entities.summary:
Czechoslovakia was a country in Central Europe created in 1918, as Czecho-Slovakia, when it declared its independence from Austria-Hungary in the aftermath of World War I. The country was formed from the union of Czechoslovakia and the Kingdom of Bohemia, with the aim of uniting the Czech and Slovak peoples under a single government.

In 1938, after the Munich Agreement, the Sudetenland became part of Nazi Germany, leading to the division of the country into the German Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia and the state of Slovakia. Between 1939 and 1945, Czechoslovakia ceased to exist, as Slovakia proclaimed its independence and Carpathian Ruthenia became part of Hungary.

The legacy of Czechoslovakia can be seen in the modern-day nations of the Czech Republic and Slovakia, which emerged from the ashes of the country after World War II. The Czechoslovakian government-in-exile played a significant role in the Allied efforts during World War II, and the country's cultural heritage continues to be celebrated in both the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

The dissolution of Czechoslovakia in 1993 marked the end of a chapter in European history, as the country peacefully transitioned to a democratic government and joined the European Union. Today, the legacy of Czechoslovakia serves as a reminder of the complex history of Central Europe and the importance of preserving cultural heritage.
